\chapter{Morning}
\label{ch:te-morning}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} in Telugu with the same word that sits inside the morning greeting.}

Say \te{ఉదయం}, Telugu's broadest morning word, note the real native competitors poddu and vēkuva, and see that Kannada splits this job across two unrelated words.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[udayam]{\te{ఉదయం} (udayam) — the same Sanskrit root, a different job than in Kannada}

\label{lesson:TE-C26-udayam}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson's \te{రోజు} was a genuine Persian surprise. This lesson's word for \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} goes the other way — straight Sanskrit, doing double duty in a way its Kannada cousin doesn't.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{ఉదయం}} (\textbf{udayam}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning}\textquotedblright{} — is a Sanskrit \textbf{tatsama}: from \textbf{\te{ఉదయ}} (\emph{udaya}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rise, appearance}\textquotedblright{}) plus Telugu's own \textbf{-\te{ము}} (\emph{-mu}) nominal suffix. This is Telugu's most common, general everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} — but be honest: it doesn't have the field entirely to itself. \textbf{\te{పొద్దు}}/\textbf{\te{పొద్దున}} (\emph{poddu}/\emph{podduna}) is genuine \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} vocabulary — cognate with Tamil \textbf{pozhudu} and Kannada \textbf{hottu} — and does real everyday work too (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{\te{పొద్దున్నే} \te{లేచాను}},\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I woke up in the morning\textquotedblright{}). \textbf{\te{వేకువ}} (\emph{vēkuva}, \textquotedblleft{}dawn, early morning\textquotedblright{}) is labeled \textbf{colloquial}, not archaic or purely poetic. \te{ఉదయం} is the broadest, most general word — but not an uncontested one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's the honest cross-language twist. Kannada also has this \textbf{exact} Sanskrit root, \textbf{\te{ఉదయ}} (\emph{udaya}) — but only inside its \textbf{greeting}, \textbf{\ka{ಶುಭೋದಯ}} (\emph{śubhōdaya}, \textquotedblleft{}good morning\textquotedblright{}). Kannada's actual everyday \textbf{noun} for \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} is a completely unrelated \textbf{native} word, \textbf{\ka{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}} (\emph{beḷagge}, \textquotedblleft{}the shining\textquotedblright{}). Telugu doesn't split the job that way: \textbf{\te{ఉదయం}} covers both the everyday noun AND, in \textbf{\te{శుభోదయం}}, the greeting root — one word, doing what Kannada spreads across two unrelated ones. And unlike \textbf{\te{రోజు}} (last lesson's genuine Persian surprise for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}), Telugu's morning word holds no such twist — straightforwardly Sanskrit, start to finish.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}udayam\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit tatsama, the broadest word, though poddu/podduna and vēkuva are real native alternatives too
  \item the cross-language twist — Kannada's \te{ఉదయ} root only shows up in ITS greeting; Telugu uses \te{ఉదయం} for both the noun and the greeting
  \item the contrast with \te{రోజు} — no Persian surprise here, just straightforward Sanskrit
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \te{ఉదయం} the ONLY word Telugu speakers use for \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — it's the broadest, most common one, but \te{పొద్దు}/\te{పొద్దున} and \te{వేకువ}, both genuinely native, do real everyday work too.) Does Kannada's everyday morning-noun share \te{ఉదయం}'s root? (\textbf{No} — Kannada's \ka{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ} is native; the shared root, udaya, shows up only inside Kannada's GREETING, \ka{ಶುಭೋದಯ}.) Does \te{ఉదయం} hold a surprise the way \te{రోజు} did? (\textbf{No} — straightforwardly Sanskrit throughout.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṛ]{\te{ఋ} — one character, met inside a word you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S129-letter-vocalic-r}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{భ} — what does it do?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ఋ}}
\textbf{\te{ఋ}} — \emph{ṛ}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape a vowel takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word. You have met that pairing twice already, at \textbf{\te{ఉ}} and at \textbf{\te{ఎ}}.

What makes this one worth a page of its own is what the vowel is. It is an \emph{r} doing a vowel's work: a whole syllable with no other vowel in it, the way English lets \emph{l} carry the second half of \emph{bottle}. Telugu took the letter from Sanskrit along with the words that need it, and modern speakers give it the sound \emph{ru}.

You already say this one, and it has \te{ఋ} at the front of its second word:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{వసంత} \te{ఋతువు}} \emph{vasanta ṛtuvu} — the spring season
\end{itemize}

\te{ఋ} is one of the rarest letters in the alphabet: outside Sanskrit borrowings it has almost nowhere to appear. Meeting it once, on a word you can already say, is enough for now.

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ఋ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ఋ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two, and say which one opens with \te{ఋ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{ఋతువు}  ·  \te{ఉదయం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ఋ} three times, saying \emph{ṛ} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vasanta ṛtuvu}, and name the letter its second word starts with
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{ఋ}? What kind of thing is it — a consonant, a vowel sign, or an independent vowel? (\textbf{An independent vowel}, sounded \emph{ru}.) Name the word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
